scope: a functional test, on a CPU toy task (a modular counter: the running sum modulo 6 of a sequence of symbols, a state that must be carried over every step), of algorithmic recurrence with a carried state (indicator RPT-1; RPT-2 is not targeted): a gated recurrent net against a parameter- and FLOP-matched causal feed-forward stack with unshared layers and against the same recurrent net with the carried state reset at every step, trained on 2 to 6 steps and judged by accuracy at 12 steps (twice the longest trained sequence), by one-sided 95% t bounds of the paired difference over the declared seeds. It makes no claim about consciousness and none about language models

Limitations: the task is a modular counter (a state-tracking problem in the cyclic group of order six), chosen because the answer needs a state carried over every step and because a small attention stack can learn it in distribution; a harder group (S3) was tried first and a feed-forward stack of the matched size did not learn it in the CPU budget, so it could not serve as a comparator; a result applies to this task family, to training on 2 to 6 steps and to evaluation at 12 steps (secondary 18 and 24), and says nothing about whether a carried state helps on language or on the experts of a Mixture of Experts (that is the GPU stage B); the feed-forward comparator is a small causal transformer (width fixed by parameter matching, standard ALiBi relative positions so that it accepts longer sequences, five layers at positional slope scale 4, pilot-selected on one pilot seed: the shallowest depth at which the stack trained on the long length reaches 0.80, which is tuning toward the extrapolation-removed control; its learning rate came from a grid of three values against two for the recurrent net, with the same warmup, optimiser and plateau rule); the stack remains optimisation-limited, 910 to 936 per mille in distribution (against 1000 for the recurrent arm) and 772 to 911 at 12 steps when trained on that length; a deeper or wider stack, a different positional scheme or a curriculum might extrapolate further; parameter and FLOP counts are matched at 6 steps, and at 12 and more steps the feed-forward stack costs more FLOPs than the recurrent net, which is reported; the saturation ceiling (980 per mille) and the share of one half in the extrapolation-removed control are not derived from the planning model; the share was loosened after exploration on pilot seed 1002 (the first criterion, that the in-length stack come within the margin of the recurrent arm, could not be met by a stack that is optimisation-limited, an empirical finding), the one-half threshold is a verbal a-priori argument, and the control is read only when the contrast is supported; the comparator class is a stack of attention layers of a fixed depth: whether it extrapolates is a known property of the class, and a COMPLETED outcome is close to a known answer (a fixed-depth stack does not count beyond the depth it was trained for); the experiment is a validated harness with a control that can fail (the stack trained on the long length), not a discovery; the reset-state ablation sees one step and so is a floor by construction on this task; beating it shows that the carried state is what the recurrent arm uses, not that recurrence beats a strong alternative (that is the feed-forward comparison); the t bounds assume roughly normal paired differences, which the declared seeds cannot check; per-seed differences, medians and both bounds are reported; the window null world (the sum of the last two steps) is easy and saturates; it guards the pipeline against an artefact that favours one family uniformly, not against a training asymmetry on hard tasks; the label-permutation control and the corrupted-input control are sensitivity controls of the pipeline: they show that a collapse to chance and a deficit of about the margin's size are resolved, not that the main effect has the size of either; an indicator property here is a functional property: the experiment says nothing about whether any system is conscious.
